name: Newton's Law of Universal Gravitation
statement: Every mass pulls every other, harder for bigger masses and much weaker with distance.
statementAccent: harder for bigger masses and much weaker with distance
meaning: Every particle of matter attracts every other with a force directly proportional to the product of their masses and inversely proportional to the square of the distance between them. The same rule governs an apple falling and the Moon orbiting the Earth — the unification of terrestrial and celestial motion often called physics' first great unification.
mechanism: The force falls off as the inverse square of distance: double the separation and the pull drops to a quarter. Newton proved that a uniform sphere attracts an outside body as if all its mass sat at its centre, which is why centre-to-centre distance is used. In modern form the force equals the gravitational constant G times the product of the masses divided by the distance squared, though Newton himself worked in geometric proportions rather than with a constant G, which is a later reformulation.

examples.text: Newton showed the inverse-square law, combined with his laws of motion, mathematically produces Kepler's three empirical laws of planetary motion — elliptical orbits, equal areas in equal times, and the period-radius relation.

Cavendish's 1797-98 torsion-balance experiment measured the faint attraction between laboratory lead spheres; his aim was the Earth's density and mass, and the value of the gravitational constant is a later derivation from his data.

Unexplained wobbles in Uranus's orbit led Le Verrier and Adams independently to predict an unseen planet using Newtonian gravity, and Galle found Neptune in 1846 within about a degree of the prediction — a triumph of the theory.

variants.name: The shell theorem
variants.text: Newton's proof that a spherically symmetric body attracts external objects as though its whole mass were concentrated at its centre, which justifies treating planets as points.

variants.name: The Cavendish experiment
variants.text: The torsion-balance measurement of gravitational attraction between known masses, the route by which the gravitational constant and the Earth's mass were later pinned down.

whyItMatters: It was the crowning achievement of the scientific revolution, uniting the fall of an apple with the motion of the planets under a single mathematical law and giving humanity its first predictive theory of the cosmos. It remains the working tool for almost all everyday and spaceflight calculations, accurate enough to send probes across the solar system.

working.lead: Scale the pull by masses and distance
working.text: expect gravitational force to grow with the product of the masses and to fall as the square of the separation.
for a spherically symmetric body, compute its gravity as if all its mass sat at its centre.

working.lead: Use it, but know its edge
working.text: rely on it for orbits and trajectories at everyday scales, while remembering general relativity governs the extreme cases.

limits: It is an extremely accurate approximation superseded, not discarded, by Einstein's general relativity in 1915, which recasts gravity as the curvature of spacetime. Newton's law fails in three tested regimes: it leaves about forty-three arcseconds per century of Mercury's perihelion precession unexplained, predicts only half the bending of light that observation confirms, and breaks down in the strong fields of black holes and neutron stars. It also poses the conceptual puzzle of action at a distance — an instantaneous force across empty space with no mechanism, which troubled Newton himself.
misreadings: It is not wrong or disproven — it remains an excellent approximation in weak fields at low speeds; it is superseded as the fundamental theory by general relativity. And the apple story, though traceable to Newton's own later recollection, does not include an apple striking his head — that detail is a later embellishment.
origin: Published by Isaac Newton in Philosophiae Naturalis Principia Mathematica (1687), whose printing was financed by Edmond Halley; Robert Hooke had suggested an inverse-square attraction in correspondence, but could not derive the orbits, and Newton's mathematical derivation was his own.
